canonical_data: Vector, halfvec, bit, and sparsevec columns in tables of the operator's own PostgreSQL database, queried with ordinary SQL predicates, joins, and transaction semantics.
current_repo_note: A PostgreSQL extension, not a server or a service. Every query runs inside a PostgreSQL database the operator runs, and the embedding pipeline, chunking, and record identity around the vectors stay with the application. Managed availability comes from hosted PostgreSQL providers that ship the extension, not from a pgvector-operated service.
strengths: Vectors live in the same tables as the rows they describe, so retrieval filters, joins, transactions, backups, and point-in-time recovery stay ordinary SQL
Reaches any language with a PostgreSQL client rather than requiring a second service and its own client library
Exact and approximate search, four vector types, six distance functions, quantization for scale, and iterative index scans for filtered queries
weaknesses: Not a retrieval product on its own: embedding, chunking, record identity, and ranking are the caller's work, and approximate indexes apply filtering after the scan
Hybrid search is a composition rather than a feature, documented as use together with PostgreSQL full-text search with fusion left to scripts in a separate repository
Approximate-index tuning (lists, probes, ef_search, scan limits) is Postgres index maintenance, so recall under filtering depends on settings the operator has to learn and watch
why_it_matters: The retrieval substrate most RAG systems in production actually sit on, published as infrastructure so the choice of vector store is visible without being mistaken for a product category, and as the counter-example to a dedicated vector database: the same retrieval inside the database the rest of the data is already in.
